newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia seen headed for early elections-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia seen headed for early elections-analysts.

text.p: Slovenia may face early elections after parliament rejected prime minister-designate Janez Drnovsek's new cabinet on Thursday, almost three months after an inconclusive November poll, analysts said on Friday.
"The possibility of premature elections in a year or two has increased," Igor Luksic, professor of politics at the Ljubljana University's Faculty of Social Sciences told Reuters.

Drnovsek of the centre-left Liberal Democrats, who formed a coalition with the ex-communist United List of Social Democrats, the pensioners' party Desus and the Nationalist Party last month, would have needed a simple majority for his line-up to be approved.

The parliamentary vote, which was taken after hours of heated debate, was split evenly with 45 votes against 45. Before the secret ballot, Drnovsek was thought to command 46 seats in the assembly after the defection of an opposition member last month.

Drnovsek, who has been acting as prime minister since April 1992, now has to present a new government line-up within 10 days. If the parliament then fails to approve at least two thirds of his ministerial candidates, President Milan Kucan will have to nominate a new prime minister.

The "Spring" alliance of three right-wing parties, which together hold 44 seats, refused to support Drnovsek's proposal, claiming his government would be unable to carry out such key tasks as winning membership of the European Union or reforming the ailing pension system.

"This has rung in a period of uncertainty. The political situation in Slovenia hampers stability at a time when decisions about Slovenia's membership in NATO and the European Union are being taken," said Drago Lavrencic, a Britain-based Slovenian political analyst.
Analysts agreed Slovenia's failure to form a new government could also have negative effects on the fledgling Slovenia bourse's liquidity.

But most said they did not expect a significant drop in the leading SBI blue-chip index, which has risen some 40 percent since the beginning of the year as foreigners poured in to snap up selected issues.

"Foreigners will continue to buy Slovenian shares but may become more careful, therefore the liquidity of the market could decrease. However, foreigners are unlikely to sell shares they already own, therefore the positive trend could continue over the year," said Toni Apollonio, an analyst at bank A Banka.
Analysts said the possibility of early elections would not severely curtail foreign investment as long as Slovenia's policy remained orientated towards joining the EU and NATO.

"Slovenia is not portrayed as a country of political risk, therefore the current political situation does not present a major influence on foreign investors," said Danilo Grasic, head of the investment sector of Slovenia's branch of Austrian bank Creditanstalt.
"The important thing is that Slovenian policy remains pro-European and pro-NATO, which is supported by all political parties," he added.

Slovenia, which gained independence from the former Yugoslavia in 1991, is widely seen as the best placed outsider to win NATO membership in the first round of the alliance's expansion, possibly before the end of the year.
The small Alpine republic signed an association agreement with the EU last year and hopes to join the 15-member group by the year 2001.
